subtitle: Generic code that works for any type, input/output as flowing streams, and errors that jump to where they can be handled.

stream.body:
Think of a stream as a river of characters between your program and the outside world. You stand on the bank and either drop things in or fish things out. cin is the input stream, cout the output, and cerr the one for errors. << inserts, >> extracts, and both chain.

The stream classes form a family tree: ios → istream/ostream → ifstream/ofstream (files) and stringstream (strings). In the figure, file streams specialise the console streams, which is inheritance from the last chapter doing real work. So ifstream is derived from which class? Read the tree.
keynotes: A stream is a sequence of characters flowing between a program and a device: cin (input), cout (output), cerr (errors).
<< inserts and >> extracts, and both chain.
The hierarchy is ios → istream/ostream → ifstream/ofstream (files) and stringstream (strings).

fmt.body:
Raw output is plain; manipulators dress it up. setw(6) sets the width, setprecision(2) with fixed sets decimals, and endl gives a newline and flushes.

Files work the same way: ofstream f("a.txt"); f << 42;. The destructor closes the file for you, which is RAII again, and you should check if (!f) after opening. As the figure shows, insertion operators chain left to right. Why can cout << a << b chain? Because each << returns the stream.
keynotes: Manipulators format output: setw(6) width, setprecision(2) with fixed, endl newline-and-flush.
ofstream f("a.txt"); f << 42; writes to a file, and the destructor closes it (RAII).

tmpl.body:
Suppose you wrote a function to find the larger of two ints, then needed it for doubles, then strings. Copy and paste three times? No. A template is a recipe the compiler follows for you: template <typename T> T maxOf(T a, T b) { return a > b ? a : b; }.

When you call maxOf(3, 9) the compiler instantiates a version with T = int, and maxOf(2.5, 1.5) another with T = double. One source, many type-specific functions, all checked at compile time with no run-time cost. The only requirement is that the type must support the operations used (here >). Until it is used, the template is only a recipe, as the figure says.
keynotes: A function template is a recipe: template <typename T> T maxOf(T a, T b).
The compiler instantiates a version for each type used: maxOf(3, 9) with T = int, maxOf(2.5, 1.5) with T = double.
It is checked at compile time with no run-time cost, and the type must support the operations used.

ctmpl.body:
The same idea works for whole classes. template <class T> class Stack { T data[100]; int top; … }; gives you Stack<int> and Stack<string> from one definition.

The Standard Template Library is this idea taken to its limit: containers (vector, list, map, set), iterators and algorithms (sort, find), all built from templates. Try it: vector<int> v = {5, 2, 9}; sort(v.begin(), v.end()); leaves the order 2, 5, 9. Three lines, no loops written by you.
keynotes: A class template such as Stack<T> gives Stack<int> and Stack<string> from one definition.
The STL supplies containers (vector, list, map, set), iterators and algorithms (sort, find), all built from templates.

exc.body:
What should a function do when it simply cannot go on, say it was asked to open a file that does not exist? Return a magic code and hope everyone checks it? Exceptions offer something better, and you will like it: the function throws an object and the runtime unwinds the call stack, destroying locals on the way, until it finds a matching catch. If none is found the program terminates.

Look at the figure: control leaps straight to the handler, and the in-between functions never resume. The shape is try { risky(); } catch (const runtime_error& e) { … }. One sensible rule: use exceptions for exceptional conditions, not ordinary control flow. And what happens to local objects while the exception propagates? They are properly destroyed.
keynotes: A function that cannot continue throws an object; the runtime unwinds the call stack, destroying locals, until it finds a matching catch.
If no handler is found the program terminates.
Use exceptions for exceptional conditions, not ordinary control flow.

safe.body:
How do you write code that survives errors without turning every function into a minefield of cleanup? Let objects do the cleaning: acquire resources in objects whose destructors release them (RAII, smart pointers) and exceptions cannot leak.

A few habits to keep. Catch by const&. Order handlers from most specific to most general, because catch (...) catches anything. And never throw from a destructor. There are three levels of guarantee: basic (no leak), strong (all-or-nothing), and no-throw.

Here is the classic mistake: put a catch (const base&) first and it swallows every derived type, hiding the specific handlers you wrote below it. So the derived exception types go before their base. Would you have spotted that?
keynotes: Acquire resources in objects whose destructors release them (RAII, smart pointers) so exceptions cannot leak.
Catch by const&, order handlers from most specific to most general, and never throw from a destructor.
Guarantee levels: basic (no leak), strong (all-or-nothing), no-throw.
Put derived exception types before their base, or the base handler swallows them.
